pos: n. (Robert Smith Candlish, 1806–1873, minister of St George's Free Church, Edinburgh, and principal of New College)
etymology: Scottish surname Candlish, a reduced form of MacCandlish, son of Cuindlis.
biblical_def: Robert S. Candlish was minister of St George's, Edinburgh, before the Disruption and of St George's Free Church after it, and on the death of Thomas Chalmers and then William Cunningham he became the acknowledged leader of the Free Church of Scotland and principal of New College. He had been one of the chief draughtsmen of the Claim of Right and he carried the established congregation's minority out in 1843 with the rest. His expository works on Genesis and on the First Epistle of John are still read, and his The Atonement defends a definite satisfaction made for the elect. In the union negotiations with the United Presbyterian Church he led the party that would not surrender the establishment principle as a term of union, holding that the civil magistrate owes a duty to the true religion that the voluntary theory denies. Act 4:19 was the Disruption's own text, whether it be right “in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God” (Act 4:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines atonement as expiation, satisfaction made by giving an equivalent, and disruption as the act of rending asunder.
webster_full: ATONE'MENT, n. Expiation; satisfaction or reparation made by giving an equivalent for an injury, or by doing or suffering that which is received in satisfaction for an offense.
DISRUP'TION, n. The act of rending asunder; the state of being rent asunder or broken in pieces by violence.
ESTAB'LISHMENT, n. Settled regulation; form; ordinance; system of laws; the episcopal or other form of religion settled by law.
scriptures: Act 4:19
But Peter and John answered and said unto them, Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye.
Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.
Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering; (for he is faithful that promised;)
Rom 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
corruption_summary: He inherited the Free Church twice over, and would not trade the establishment principle for a union.
corruption_paragraphs: Candlish is the figure through whom the Disruption's principle passed into the next generation. The question of 1843 was never whether the church should be established; it was whether a civil court could install a minister over a congregation that had rejected him, and so govern the church's spiritual acts. Act 4:19 and Act 5:29 are the apostolic answer, that “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29) when the two commands collide, and Rom 13:1 keeps the magistrate's own authority intact in its own sphere.

In the union controversy Candlish refused the voluntary position, which holds that the state owes religion nothing but non-interference. The dictionary's own standard is the classical two-kingdoms doctrine of the Reformers: family, church, and state are three God-ordained authorities, each with a proper sphere, and the magistrate is not religiously neutral even though he may not govern the church. 1Jn 4:1 requires the trying of spirits, and the voluntary theory, like the Erastian one it opposed, settles by a formula a question Scripture settles by distinguishing jurisdictions.
roots_summary: Greek hupakouo / peitharcheo (G3980), to obey authority; dokimazo (G1381), to try, prove; exousia (G1849), authority.
roots_lines: Greek enopion (G1799) — in the sight of, before; Acts 4:19.
Greek peitharcheo (G3980) — to obey one in authority; Acts 5:29.
Greek dokimazo (G1381) — to try, prove, test; 1 John 4:1.
usage: “in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God” (Act 4:19) — the Disruption's question.
“We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29) — its answer.
“the powers that be are ordained of God” (Rom 13:1) — the magistrate's own sphere, untouched.

pos: n. (Patrick Fairbairn, 1805–1874, first principal of the Free Church College, Glasgow, author of The Typology of Scripture)
etymology: Scottish surname Fairbairn, fair child; Patrick, from Latin patricius, nobleman.
biblical_def: Patrick Fairbairn served parishes in Orkney and Berwickshire, came out at the Disruption, and became professor at Aberdeen and then the first principal of the Free Church College in Glasgow. His Typology of Scripture is the standard nineteenth-century Reformed treatment of the subject: he argued that the types of the Old Testament are divinely intended prefigurations, not devotional analogies invented by later readers, and he laid down controls for distinguishing a real type from a fanciful one — that it must have a genuine historical existence, a real correspondence in substance, and some warrant in the New Testament's own handling of it. He also wrote Prophecy Viewed in Respect to Its Distinctive Nature and a Hermeneutical Manual, and edited the Imperial Bible Dictionary. Luk 24:27 is the method's charter: Christ expounded “in all the scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luk 24:27).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a type as an emblem or figure of something to come, and hermeneutics as the art of interpretation.
webster_full: TYPE, n. The figure of something to come; as, Abraham's sacrifice and the paschal lamb, were types of Christ. A sign; a symbol; an emblem.
HERMENEU'TICS, n. The art or science of interpretation, particularly of the Holy Scriptures.
PROPH'ECY, n. A foretelling; prediction; a declaration of something to come.
scriptures: And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.
Joh 5:39
Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me.
For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
corruption_summary: He gave typology rules, which is what kept it from becoming allegory.
corruption_paragraphs: Typology has two ditches. On one side is the allegorising habit that finds Christ in every detail of the tabernacle hardware and so makes the interpreter's ingenuity the authority. On the other is the critical habit that denies divine intention in the Old Testament altogether, so that the New Testament writers are read as imposing meanings the text never carried. Fairbairn cut between them by requiring a real historical institution, a substantial correspondence, and apostolic warrant. Joh 5:39 supplies the premise: the scriptures “are they which testify of me” (Joh 5:39).

The corruption to name is the modern academic treatment of typology as a literary strategy of the early church rather than a feature of the text. If 2Pe 1:21 is true and holy men spoke as they were moved by the Holy Ghost, then the Author of the earlier book intended the later fulfilment, and the type is objectively there to be found. Isa 8:20 supplies the restraint in the other direction: an interpretation that cannot be brought to the law and the testimony is the interpreter's invention, however edifying it sounds.
roots_summary: Greek tupos (G5179), a type, pattern; skia (G4639), a shadow; diermeneuo (G1329), to expound.
roots_lines: Greek tupos (G5179) — a figure, pattern, type; Romans 5:14.
Greek martureo (G3140) — to bear witness, testify; John 5:39.
Greek phero (G5342) — to bear, be moved; 2 Peter 1:21.
usage: “in all the scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luk 24:27) — typology's charter.
“they are they which testify of me” (Joh 5:39) — the types are in the text.
“To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) — the restraint on ingenuity.

pos: n. (James Begg, 1808–1883, minister of Newington Free Church, Edinburgh, editor of the Watchword, defender of exclusive psalmody and the establishment principle)
biblical_def: James Begg was minister of Newington Free Church in Edinburgh for thirty-eight years and the most persistent controversialist the Free Church produced. He founded and edited the Watchword as the organ of the constitutional party, and fought on four fronts at once: against the proposed union with the United Presbyterians on the ground that it required abandoning the establishment principle; against the introduction of hymns of human composition into public worship; against instrumental accompaniment; and against the softening of the church's testimony on the Sabbath. His position on worship was the regulative principle applied strictly: what God has commanded in corporate worship is required, and what He has not commanded is not permitted, so the church sings the Psalms He gave. Deu 12:32 is the rule, “thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it” (Deu 12:32).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a psalm as a sacred song or hymn, and psalmody as the act or practice of singing sacred songs.
webster_full: PSALM, n. A sacred song or hymn; a song composed on a divine subject and in praise of God.
PSALM'ODY, n. The act, practice or art of singing sacred songs.
WOR'SHIP, n. Chiefly and eminently, the act of paying divine honors to the Supreme Being.
scriptures: What thing soever I command you, observe to do it: thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
Joh 4:24
God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.
Rom 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
corruption_summary: He spent four decades insisting that worship is governed by command and not by preference.
corruption_paragraphs: Begg was called narrow in his lifetime and the charge has stuck, but his argument is harder to answer than his manner was to like. If corporate worship is a matter of divine prescription, then the burden lies on whoever introduces an element to show the warrant; if it is a matter of edification judged by the congregation, then the regulative principle has been abandoned and the only remaining limit is taste. Joh 4:24 names what God requires, worship “in spirit and in truth” (Joh 4:24), and 1Co 14:40 requires order under command.

The dictionary holds the regulative principle and therefore grants Begg his premise, while noting that his own church came to a different conclusion on psalmody and that the question of hymns of human composition is not settled by Deu 12:32 alone. The corruption he saw coming has arrived in a form worse than hymnody: a worship service designed around the preferences of the attender, in which the question of command is not asked at all. On the union question he was outvoted and his successors inherited his argument, which is the usual fate of the constitutional party in a declining church.
roots_summary: Hebrew yacaph (H3254), to add; gara' (H1639), to diminish; Greek euschemonos (G2156), decently.
roots_lines: Hebrew gara' (H1639) — to diminish, take away; Deuteronomy 12:32.
usage: “thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it” (Deu 12:32) — his rule for worship.
“worship him in spirit and in truth” (Joh 4:24) — the two requirements.
“Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40) — order under command.

pos: n. (Hugh Miller, 1802–1856, Cromarty stonemason, geologist, and editor of The Witness, the Free Church newspaper)
etymology: English occupational surname Miller, one who grinds grain; Hugh, from Germanic hug, mind, spirit.
biblical_def: Hugh Miller was a stonemason from Cromarty who taught himself geology from the quarries he worked and became the most widely read scientific writer in Scotland. The Old Red Sandstone and The Testimony of the Rocks were written in a prose that carried fossil fish and Devonian strata into ordinary households. At the Disruption he was made editor of The Witness, the Free Church's Edinburgh newspaper, and his leading articles did as much as any pulpit to carry the church's case to the Scottish public. He held that the geological record is of great antiquity and read the days of Genesis as long periods or as a sequence of prophetic visions, arguing the position against both the sceptics who used geology against Scripture and the developmentalists of the Vestiges school. He died by his own hand in December 1856, under an illness of the brain that his physicians certified. Job 38:4 is the question his whole subject stands under, “Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?” (Job 38:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines geology as the science of the structure of the earth, and a fossil as a substance dug out of the earth.
webster_full: GEOL'OGY, n. The doctrine or science of the structure of the earth or terraqueous globe, and of the substances which compose it.
FOS'SIL, n. A substance dug from the earth; in modern usage, the petrified remains of plants and animals.
STRA'TUM, n. A bed; a layer; a course; as a stratum of sand, of clay, or of earth.
scriptures: Job 38:4
Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? declare, if thou hast understanding.
O LORD, how manifold are thy works! in wisdom hast thou made them all: the earth is full of thy riches.
Rom 1:20
For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse:
Gen 1:1
In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
corruption_summary: The Free Church's best writer was a self-taught quarryman who read the rocks and would not read them against Scripture.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary's own position on Genesis is six literal days of twenty-four hours, and Miller did not hold it; he read the days as long ages and later as a series of visions shown to Moses. That reading is not the dictionary's voice. It is, however, the old-earth position within the Reformed line rather than a concession to unbelief, and Miller's entire purpose in holding it was apologetic: he was answering men who used the strata to argue that Scripture is a fable, and he never once granted that the record of the rocks may overrule the record of revelation.

What is worth recovering is the target of his heaviest fire. Vestiges of the Natural History of Creation had just proposed a universal development of life by natural law, and Miller attacked it from the fossil evidence itself, showing that the record exhibits sudden fully-formed appearances rather than the gradual ascent the theory required. Rom 1:20 is the ground he stood on, that the invisible things of God are “clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made” (Rom 1:20). His death was the end of a diagnosed illness and the dictionary records it plainly and without verdict, as the Free Church did when it buried him in the Grange with his elders carrying the coffin.
roots_summary: Hebrew yacad (H3245), to found, establish; rab (H7227), many, manifold; Greek poiema (G4161), a thing made.
roots_lines: Hebrew yacad (H3245) — to found, lay a foundation; Job 38:4.
Greek poiema (G4161) — a thing made, workmanship; Romans 1:20.
usage: “Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?” (Job 38:4) — the question over the quarry.
“in wisdom hast thou made them all” (Psa 104:24) — what he saw in the strata.
“clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made” (Rom 1:20) — his apologetic ground.

pos: n. (Alexander Moody Stuart, 1809–1898, minister of Free St Luke's, Edinburgh, biographer of John Duncan and advocate of the mission to the Jews)
etymology: Greek Alexandros, defender of men; Scottish surnames Moody and Stuart, the latter from steward.
biblical_def: Alexander Moody Stuart ministered at St Luke's in Edinburgh for more than fifty years, coming out at the Disruption with his congregation. He was one of the Free Church's steadiest advocates of the mission to the Jews, which that church took up from its first year, and he travelled and wrote for it. He published a careful exposition of the Song of Solomon, read as the Scriptures read it, of Christ and His church rather than as a collection of love lyrics; The Three Marys; and the standard Life of John Duncan, preserving the sayings of the Hebraist whom Scotland called Rabbi Duncan. He was a friend of revival and a critic of the machinery of it, holding that awakening is given and not produced. Isa 49:6 is the text the Jewish mission rested on, that the Servant is given “for a light to the Gentiles” (Isa 49:6) without the tribes of Jacob being forgotten.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a mission as a sending, a commission, and allegory as a figurative sentence or discourse.
webster_full: MIS'SION, n. A sending or being sent, usually the latter; a being sent or delegated by authority, with certain powers for transacting business.
AL'LEGORY, n. A figurative sentence or discourse, in which the principal subject is described by another subject resembling it in its properties and circumstances.
AWA'KENING, n. A revival of religion, or more general attention to spiritual concerns than usual.
scriptures: Isa 49:6

And he said, It is a light thing that thou shouldest be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give thee for a light to the Gentiles, that thou mayest be my salvation unto the end of the earth.
Psa 67:2
That thy way may be known upon earth, thy saving health among all nations.
Act 1:8

But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth.
Joh 4:24
God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.
corruption_summary: Fifty years in one Edinburgh pulpit, the Song read of Christ, and the Jews not forgotten.
corruption_paragraphs: The Free Church's mission to the Jews was begun in its first years and Moody Stuart was among its most persistent friends. The warrant is not sentiment. Psa 67:2 asks that God's way be known upon earth, “thy saving health among all nations” (Psa 67:2), and Isa 49:6 places the restoring of the preserved of Israel and the light to the Gentiles in one commission. Act 1:8 orders the witness from Jerusalem outward, not away from it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is his handling of the Song of Solomon. Modern commentary generally reads it as human love poetry and treats the older reading as pious imposition; Moody Stuart read it as the church has read it, of Christ and His bride, while refusing the allegorising excesses that find doctrine in every ornament. The second thing to recover is his estimate of revival: he prayed for awakening and would not manufacture it, which is the same discipline Joh 4:24 imposes on worship.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'or (H216), light; yeshu'ah (H3444), salvation, saving health; Greek martus (G3144), a witness.
usage: “for a light to the Gentiles” (Isa 49:6) — the Jewish mission's warrant.
“thy saving health among all nations” (Psa 67:2) — the prayer behind it.
“ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem” (Act 1:8) — outward, not away.

pos: n. (Thomas Guthrie, 1803–1873, minister of Free St John's, Edinburgh, founder of the ragged schools)
etymology: Scottish surname Guthrie, from the lands of Guthrie in Angus.
biblical_def: Thomas Guthrie ministered in the Cowgate and the West Port of Edinburgh, among the poorest closes in Britain, and came out at the Disruption to Free St John's. In 1847 he published A Plea for Ragged Schools, arguing that the city's destitute children, who were not received in ordinary schools and were being raised into crime, should be fed, taught, and given a trade at the public cost and the church's hand. The pamphlet and its sequels founded the Edinburgh Original Ragged Industrial Schools and the movement spread through Scotland and England. He was also the leading platform speaker of the Scottish temperance cause, and moderator of the Free Church assembly in 1862. Luk 14:13 was the pattern he preached and practised, that the feast is for “the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind” (Luk 14:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ragged as rough with sharp projections, tattered, and destitute as needy, not having the necessary means.
webster_full: RAG'GED, a. Rent or worn into tatters, or having loose shreds; wearing tattered clothes.
DES'TITUTE, a. Needy; abject; comfortless; wanting necessaries; not having the necessary means.
CHAR'ITY, n. In a general sense, love, benevolence, good will; that disposition of heart which inclines men to think favorably of their fellow men, and to do them good.
scriptures: But when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind:
And the King shall answer and say unto them, Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.
Jas 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
Psa 82:3
Defend the poor and fatherless: do justice to the afflicted and needy.
corruption_summary: He wrote a pamphlet about the children in the Edinburgh closes, and schools opened across two countries.
corruption_paragraphs: Guthrie's case is worth setting out because it was argued and not merely felt. He showed from the police records that the children of the closes were passing into the prisons at a predictable rate, that the ordinary schools would not take them, and that it was cheaper as well as righteous to feed and teach them. Jas 1:27 defines pure religion as visiting “the fatherless and widows in their affliction” (Jas 1:27), which is a visit, not a sentiment, and Psa 82:3 commands the defence of the poor and fatherless as a matter of justice.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the order Guthrie kept. He fed and taught the children and he preached to them; he did not treat the one as a substitute for the other, and he did not treat the gospel as a means to social improvement or social improvement as a means to a hearing. Mat 25:40 makes the care of the least a service rendered to Christ Himself, which is a reason that does not depend on results.
roots_summary: Greek ptochos (G4434), poor, beggarly; thlipsis (G2347), affliction; Hebrew yathom (H3490), fatherless.
usage: “call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind” (Luk 14:13) — the ragged-school charter.
“the fatherless and widows in their affliction” (Jas 1:27) — a visit, not a sentiment.
“one of the least of these my brethren” (Mat 25:40) — a reason independent of results.

pos: n. (John Eadie, 1810–1876, United Presbyterian minister and professor, commentator on Paul's epistles)
biblical_def: John Eadie was a Secession and then United Presbyterian minister in Glasgow who combined a large city pastorate with the work of a professional exegete. He taught biblical literature in his church's divinity hall for thirty-three years and produced the Greek-text commentaries on Ephesians, Colossians, Philippians, Galatians, and Thessalonians that English readers used before Lightfoot: close, grammatical, patient with the particles, and theologically Reformed without being polemical in the notes. He compiled the Biblical Cyclopaedia and a dictionary of the Bible that went through many editions, wrote the history of the English translations, and served on the New Testament company of the Revised Version. 2Ti 2:15 is the whole description of his working life, a workman “rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15), and Act 20:27 the measure of what he believed a commentary was for.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a commentator as one who writes annotations, and a lexicon as a dictionary, a vocabulary of a language.
webster_full: COM'MENTATOR, n. One who writes notes upon the works of another, to illustrate his writings, or to explain obscure passages.
LEX'ICON, n. A dictionary; a vocabulary or book containing an alphabetical arrangement of the words in a language.
VER'SION, n. A translation; the rendering of a passage or a book from one language into another.
scriptures: Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God.
Eph 4:11
And he gave some, apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers;
Col 1:28
Whom we preach, warning every man, and teaching every man in all wisdom; that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus:
corruption_summary: A city pastor who wrote the grammatical commentaries English readers needed, and let the grammar carry the doctrine.
corruption_paragraphs: Eadie's commentaries illustrate a discipline that has largely been lost: the conviction that doctrine is established by the grammar and not imported alongside it. He works through the Greek of Ephesians clause by clause and the Reformed conclusions arrive because the text yields them. Act 20:27 is the standard, that nothing of the counsel of God be shunned, and a commentator who skips the hard clause has shunned something.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the pairing of pastorate and exegesis in one man. Eph 4:11 gives pastors and teachers as one gift, and Col 1:28 describes the aim as presenting every man perfect in Christ. The modern separation, in which the commentary is written by a specialist who preaches to nobody and the sermon is preached by a pastor who reads no Greek, is a loss on both sides. Eadie was a United Presbyterian rather than a Free Churchman, which is a reminder that the Disruption generation's scholarship was not confined to one of Scotland's churches.
roots_summary: Greek orthotomeo (G3718), to cut straight; hupostellomai (G5288), to withdraw, shun; didaskalos (G1320), a teacher.
roots_lines: Greek orthotomeo (G3718) — to cut straight, rightly divide; 2 Timothy 2:15.
Greek hupostellomai (G5288) — to draw back, shun; Acts 20:27.
usage: “rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15) — his working life in five words.
“I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God” (Act 20:27) — no clause skipped.
“some, pastors and teachers” (Eph 4:11) — one gift, not two professions.

pos: n. (James Bannerman, 1807–1868, professor at New College, Edinburgh, author of The Church of Christ)
biblical_def: James Bannerman was minister at Ormiston and Montrose, came out at the Disruption, and in 1849 became professor of apologetics and then of pastoral theology at New College, Edinburgh. His lectures were published after his death as The Church of Christ, two volumes which remain the fullest Reformed treatment of ecclesiology in English: the nature and attributes of the visible church, the power of the keys and its limits, the subjects and administration of the sacraments, the office-bearers, the relation of church and state, and the authority of church courts. He argued throughout that the church's power is wholly ministerial and declarative — she announces and applies what Christ has legislated and has no power to legislate herself. Mat 16:18 gives the builder and the building, and Act 20:28 gives the officers their charge, to feed the church “which he hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ecclesiastical as pertaining to the church, and the keys as the emblem of the power of binding and loosing.
webster_full: ECCLESIAS'TICAL, a. Pertaining or relating to the church; as ecclesiastical discipline or government; ecclesiastical affairs or history.
KEY, n. In Scripture, the emblem of power or authority; as, the keys of the kingdom of heaven.
MINISTE'RIAL, a. Pertaining to ministry or service; acting as an instrument or agent, not with original authority.
scriptures: And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
But if I tarry long, that thou mayest know how thou oughtest to behave thyself in the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth.
And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican.
corruption_summary: The church's power is ministerial and declarative: she applies Christ's law and cannot make her own.
corruption_paragraphs: Bannerman's distinction is the key to the whole subject. A legislative power would make the church the source of her own constitution; a ministerial and declarative power makes her the administrator of a constitution already given. Mat 16:18 settles the matter of ownership in Christ's own words, “upon this rock I will build my church” (Mat 16:18), and Act 20:28 fixes the purchase price. Officers of a purchased flock do not own it.

Two corruptions are foreclosed by the same distinction. Rome claims a legislative magisterium and so can bind consciences on doctrines Scripture does not teach; the Erastian arrangement the Disruption refused lets the civil court exercise the keys from outside. Mat 18:17 locates discipline in the church, and 1Ti 3:15 calls her the pillar and ground of the truth — the pillar that holds the truth up, not the quarry the truth is cut from. Bannerman's volumes are the Free Church's settled answer to both, and the dictionary follows him.
roots_summary: Greek oikodomeo (G3618), to build; episkopos (G1985), overseer; peripoieomai (G4046), to purchase, acquire.
roots_lines: Greek oikodomeo (G3618) — to build, build up; Matthew 16:18.
usage: “upon this rock I will build my church” (Mat 16:18) — whose church it is.
“which he hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28) — the price, and so the charge.
“tell it unto the church” (Mat 18:17) — where discipline sits.

pos: n. (Andrew Mitchell Thomson, 1779–1831, minister of St George's, Edinburgh, leader of the Apocrypha controversy and of immediate abolition)
etymology: Greek Andreas, manly; Scottish patronymic Thom-son, son of Thomas.
biblical_def: Andrew Thomson was minister of St George's, Edinburgh, from 1814, editor of the Christian Instructor, and the dominant evangelical voice in the Church of Scotland in the generation before the Disruption. Two controversies made him. In the first he discovered that the British and Foreign Bible Society was circulating Bibles on the continent with the Apocrypha bound in and interspersed among the canonical books, and he fought the practice until the Society resolved to circulate the canonical Scriptures alone; the Edinburgh Bible Society separated over it. In the second he broke with the gradualists of the anti-slavery movement and argued for immediate and total emancipation, on the ground that a thing forbidden by God is not to be phased out on a timetable. He died suddenly at fifty-two, and his pulpit passed in time to Candlish. Deu 4:2 is the Apocrypha argument, and Exo 21:16 the other.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines apocrypha as books whose authors are not known, not admitted into the sacred canon, and canon as a rule, the genuine books of Scripture.
webster_full: APOC'RYPHA, n. Books whose authors are not known; books appended to the sacred Scriptures, but being of doubtful origin, are not esteemed canonical.
CAN'ON, n. In an ecclesiastical sense, a law or rule of doctrine or discipline; the genuine books of the Holy Scriptures, called the sacred canon.
EMANCIPA'TION, n. The act of setting free from servitude or slavery; deliverance from bondage.
scriptures: Deu 4:2
Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it, that ye may keep the commandments of the LORD your God which I command you.
For I testify unto every man that heareth the words of the prophecy of this book, If any man shall add unto these things, God shall add unto him the plagues that are written in this book:
And he that stealeth a man, and selleth him, or if he be found in his hand, he shall surely be put to death.
Isa 58:6
Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke?
corruption_summary: He got the Apocrypha out of the Bible Society's Bibles and refused a timetable for emancipation.
corruption_paragraphs: The Apocrypha controversy looks like a quarrel over bookbinding and is a question about the canon. A Bible in which Tobit and Maccabees stand between Nehemiah and Esther teaches the reader, without a word of argument, that these books have the same standing as the rest. Deu 4:2 forbids adding to the word that God commanded, and Rev 22:18 pronounces the warning at the other end of the canon. Thomson was accused of harshness toward a benevolent society; he was defending the sixty-six books.

On slavery his position was the one the dictionary holds and the one most of his contemporaries would not take. Gradual emancipation treats a sin as an institution to be wound down; Exo 21:16 fixes a capital penalty on manstealing, and Isa 58:6 commands the loosing of the bands of wickedness, to “let the oppressed go free” (Isa 58:6), with no clause allowing for a transitional period. The corruption to name is the respectable moderation that grants a wrong is a wrong and then schedules its end for a generation that will not have to pay for it.
roots_summary: Hebrew yacaph (H3254), to add; ganab (H1589), to steal; chophshi (H2670), free.
roots_lines: Greek epitithemi (G2007) — to add to, lay upon; Revelation 22:18.
usage: “Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you” (Deu 4:2) — the Apocrypha argument.
“he that stealeth a man, and selleth him” (Exo 21:16) — why not gradually.
“let the oppressed go free” (Isa 58:6) — no transitional clause.

pos: n. (William Arnot, 1808–1875, Free Church minister in Glasgow and Edinburgh, author of Laws from Heaven for Life on Earth)
etymology: Scottish surname Arnot, from the lands of Arnot in Fife.
biblical_def: William Arnot was a ploughman's son who worked as a gardener before the university, ministered at St Peter's in Glasgow and then at the Free High Church in Edinburgh, and was moderator of the Free Church assembly in 1869. He is remembered for his expositions, chiefly Laws from Heaven for Life on Earth, a two-series treatment of the Proverbs which takes each sentence as a law of God governing ordinary conduct — money, speech, labour, the household, the sluggard, the surety — and refuses to leave it at the level of prudential advice. He also wrote on the parables and a memoir of James Hamilton, and travelled for the Free Church in America and the East. Pro 1:7 is the hinge of the whole book he expounded: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge” (Pro 1:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a proverb as a short sentence often repeated, expressing a well known truth, and prudence as wisdom applied to practice.
webster_full: PROV'ERB, n. A short sentence often repeated, expressing a well known truth or common fact, ascertained by experience or observation; a maxim of wisdom.
PRU'DENCE, n. Wisdom applied to practice; that discernment which enables a person to judge critically of what is correct in conduct.
DIS'CIPLINE, n. Education; instruction; cultivation and improvement, comprehending instruction in arts, sciences, correct sentiments and morals.
scriptures: Pro 1:7
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge: but fools despise wisdom and instruction.
Pro 9:10
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding.
Pro 22:6
Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.
The heart of the prudent getteth knowledge; and the ear of the wise seeketh knowledge.
corruption_summary: He read the Proverbs as laws from heaven, not as shrewd advice that happens to be in the Bible.
corruption_paragraphs: Arnot's title is his argument. The Proverbs are commonly read as a collection of worldly wisdom, useful but not binding, and read that way they become a self-help manual with a religious frame. He read them as divine law applied to the ordinary business of a week, and so expounded the sayings on the surety, the sluggard, the tale-bearer, and the false balance as obligations rather than observations. Pro 9:10 supplies the reason the book cannot be detached from its root: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (Pro 9:10).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that practical wisdom is not a lower order of revelation. Pro 22:6 on the training of a child and Pro 18:15 on the getting of knowledge are the same divine voice as the prophets, addressed to the household and the shop. A church that preaches doctrine on the Lord's Day and leaves conduct to common sense through the week has split what Proverbs joins, and Arnot's two series were written against exactly that habit.
roots_summary: Hebrew yir'ah (H3374), fear, reverence; chokmah (H2451), wisdom; mashal (H4912), a proverb, parable.
roots_lines: Hebrew chanak (H2596) — to train up, dedicate; Proverbs 22:6.
Hebrew bin (H995) — to discern, be prudent; Proverbs 18:15.
usage: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge” (Pro 1:7) — the hinge of the book.
“The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (Pro 9:10) — and of its practice.
“Train up a child in the way he should go” (Pro 22:6) — law, not advice.
